News.title: Two dead including US state legislator in fireball plane crash after plummeting into park as tributes flood in
News.content:
A NORTH Dakota state legislator and a pilot have been killed in a fiery single-engine plane crash as tributes begin to pour in.

Liz Conmy died after the plane she was travelling on smashed down into a suburban park shortly after takeoff.





Dramatic driveway CCTV from a nearby home captured the moment the plane plummeted and exploded into a fiery ball.

It’s understood the plane had just left Crystal Airport on Saturday morning when it crashed down into a green space in Brooklyn Park, north of Minneapolis.

Emergency services raced to the small park to find the wreckage engulfed in flames.



Debris was scattered across the park as smoke could be seen rising from the wreckage.

Crews extinguished the fire but neither Conmy nor the pilot — who has not yet been identified — could be saved.

Radar records show the plane took off at 11.30 am and was travelling north before disappearing from tracking systems.

Just 20 minutes later, cops were notified of the horror smash from terrified bystanders.



Fortunately no other injuries were reported.

Tributes are pouring in for Conmy who was a representative for the North Dakota Democratic–Nonpartisan League Party which is an affiliate of the national Democratic Party.

“We are completely heartbroken and gutted by the loss of Representative Liz Conmy. Her death is a profound loss for our state,” the party said in a statement.

She is being remembered for being a champion for public education, the environment and transparency.

The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed two people were aboard.



The National Transportation Safety Board said it is investigating a crash involving a Beech F33A airplane.

The area is expected to be closed for a few days while investigations continue.

Crystal Airport was closed after the crash but operations have since resumed.

News.title: Heroic moment Secret Service agents pin down ‘Trump dinner gunman’ after shootout in Washington hotel lobby
News.content:
THIS is the moment the “coward” suspected gunman who charged a White House Correspondents’ Dinner is arrested by hero Secret Service agents.

Dramatic footage shows agents holding Cole Tomas Allen, 31, on the ground after the alleged gunman charged through a security cordon outside the prestigious event.





Dramatic footage shows agents pinning the suspected shooter to the ground.

A second video shows the suspected shooter lying face down outside the Washington Hilton with his hands tied behind his back.

Allen is pinned down on the ground, covered in a foil blanket.



FBI agents raided the suspected shooter’s California home, as the Secret Service blasted him as a “coward”.

The 31-year-old is facing firearms and assault charges after he was arrested.

It comes as…

He was reportedly staying at the hotel at the time of the shooting.



Overnight, heavily armed agents swarmed a home in Torrance, California, linked to Allen.

And chilling video from Donald Trump’s correspondents’ dinner shows the president and his wife sat at the dais at the front of the Washington Hilton as a shooting broke out in the venue.

Trump recalled how his wife alerted him to the sound of gunshots in a briefing to the press just an hour later.

“The fact that we were sitting next to each other, the First Lady on my right, and I heard a noise,” Trump said.

The US president added that at first he thought it was a tray being dropped on the floor by a staff member.



Melania was the first to raise the alarm that the sound could be gunfire, Trump added.

The First Lady told her husband about the “bad noise”, as Trump added: “it was a rather traumatic experience for her”.

“Melania was very cognisant,” he continued.



“The First Lady was doing a terrific job. She loves the country.

“She recognises it better than any. But she told me numerous times, she said ‘you are in a dangerous job’.”

In the video, Secret Service agents storm the stage as Melania ducks beneath the table.

Officers then take the president to the ground before bundling him off the stage.

Agents with full tactical gear scan the room as their guns are cocked ready to fire.



Melania and Karoline can be seen crawling backstage as they flee for their lives.

News.title: Blueprint for new UK ‘village community’ across eight fields with affordable homes is unveiled
News.content:
PLANS for a new UK village featuring a number of affordable homes have officially been unveiled.

The proposal outlines a “village community” development built across eight fields, featuring green spaces and play areas alongside the residential spaces.





The development, known as Penn an Vre, will include up to 300 new homes, along with a community hub, parking, landscaping, and public realm works.

Persimmon Homes has applied for outline planning permission to build a “village community”, connected via internal estate roads.

If approved, the new village will be constructed on the outskirts of a Cornish town, on land west of Latchbrook Farm, Trematon, near Saltash.

A planning statement says: “Penn an Vre will be a village community for up to 300 new high-quality homes.

“Drawing on local influences and surrounding resources, this village will offer residents a place to live within a beautiful landscape at the ‘Gateway to Cornwall’.”

According to the blueprint, the eight-field site will provide a “strategic urban extension” to the west of Saltash.

Homes in Penn an Vre would be served by bus links into the town centre, as well as further destinations, including Plymouth city centre, Liskeard, and Callington.

Plans outline the 300 new residential units, which would range from apartments to four-bed homes, with 30 per cent provided as affordable homes.



The blueprint also show a central green space, green links, community kitchen gardens with raised planters to promote local food growing, a social space designed specifically for teenagers, and a community orchard.

News.title: We live next door to ‘Real Slim Shady’… he and his ‘XL Bullies’ have left us scared to even step outside our own homes
News.content:
GUESS WHO'S BACK? We live next door to ‘Real Slim Shady’… he and his ‘XL Bullies’ have left us scared to even step outside our own homes

AN INFAMOUS yob who renamed himself after Eminem turned a once quiet street into a “living nightmare” leaving locals scared to step outside.

Neighbours say they have endured three years of misery fuelled by chaotic behaviour, intimidation and his two “XL Bully” dogs “running wild”.





Marshall Mathers, previously known as Glen Dowsey and Colin Dowsey, moved into Newick Road in Brighton after already being branded one of the city’s biggest louts

His notoriety was well known – having a slew of convictions for thuggery over the last decade and a half.

He famously staged a bizarre rooftop protest in 2018 at a BrewDog pub that sparked a city shutdown as he hurled tiles at police during a 10-hour siege.



And other convictions since have included racially aggravated assault, criminal damage and being found in possession of an axe.

Locals insist life next door to the “Real Slim Shady” has been a living hell – and have welcomed the council and cops now booting him out.

They said Mathers’ let his dogs run wild, was abusive, threatening and left neighbours in constant fear.

But now – for the summer at least – residents on Newick Road in Brighton will have peace after the council said enough was enough and booted him out.



A court order has barred Mathers from returning for three months and his flat has been boarded up.

The closure order was issued on April 14 – and says it was on the grounds of anti-social behaviour, persistent disorder and serious nuisance.

And during The Sun’s visit to the road – Mathers himself showed up, sparking fury from locals.

Two neighbours called the police – and when confronted by our reporter, serial troublemaker Mathers told us to “f*** off”.

Many locals recalled the street erupting into chaos last August when Mathers was locked in another stand-off with police.



Armed cops swarmed the quiet road in a three-hour showdown with Mathers who locked himself in the now shuttered flat.

Hamish Mackenzie, 74, has lived on the road for 45 years.

He said: “I have never had any issues or aggro like this until he arrived.

“We have had three years of it and it’s absolute hell.”

Mathers’s dogs – described by locals as XL Bullies – were reportedly removed from the property after this confrontation.



Alex Courtney, 34, who has lived on the street for 14 years, said her family were dragged into the terrifying confrontation.

“My other half went to try to defuse the situation,” she said.



“Armed police rocked up and pinned my boyfriend to the floor thinking it was him while Marshall was hiding inside his flat and locked the door.”

After that flashpoint, fear gripped the street as they begged the council and police to take action.

Alex said: “And after that situation we couldn’t use the front garden without him shouting at us or his dogs running at us.

“We don’t need this, I have a two year old, it’s just not fair,” she said.

“He has made everybody’s life hell. It used to be such a lovely neighbourhood we all look out for each other.



“But we had him disrupting the harmony. I really hope the council reconsider the three months, it has to be a permanent expulsion.”

Pensioner Jackie Funnell, 81, who lives a couple of doors down, said the change since he was booted out is stark.

“It is heaven without him. The door was open all day yesterday and it will be today until he is back,” she told The Sun.

“If he comes back I will leave. I have been here for about 50 years. I like it here, I have friends here. But if he comes back I’ll have to go.

“I don’t want to go, I am too old to start all over again and go about making new friends in a new area.”



She said one terrifying encounter saw the dogs burst into her home.

“I came back one day from the knitting group and the dog charged at me. It was terrifying. We have been putting up with this for years,” Jackie said.

“Frankly, I am at the end of my tether, I am an elderly lady, don’t I deserve some peace?”



Neighbour and Brighton and Hove Albion fan Alan Ingram, 87, questioned why Mathers was even housed there in the first place.

“They have only slung him out for three months. But after the chaos he has caused here, how can they let him back?” he said.

“Seems mad to me, and if he does come back, he won’t be welcomed.”

Fellow nearby resident, Sonya Bonner, claimed Mathers was “alright”, although she doesn’t approve of how he treated her neighbours.



“I’ve never had a problem with Marshall. I have heard stuff. I don’t judge people,” she said.

“He is always polite to me, says ‘good morning’ and smiles at me. He has always been all right with me.

“I keep myself to myself. But many other people won’t have quite such nice things to say, and he has certainly done some bad things here.”

Mathers briefly returned to Newick Road, opening the gate to his flat before heading upstairs to a neighbour’s property.

When approached for comment, he snapped: “F**k off I don’t want to talk to your sh*t newspaper.”



Appalled and astonished by his return, Jackie hissed: “He has got the nerve of a devil to come back here.”

Two neighbours immediately called police, claiming he had breached the court order by returning to the street.

Though Sussex Police told The Sun that Mathers attending a neighbouring flat “does not constitute a breach of the closure order”.

When asked why Mathers had popped in for just a couple of minutes, the neighbour said it was to ask if he had any “dog ends” he could have.



The Sun put the locals’ concerns to Brighton and Hove Council – including calls for him to be permanently banned from returning.

A spokesperson said: “We understand the distress and disruption this situation has caused the community and apologise for the time it took to resolve.

“Unfortunately, the hearing was delayed by court backlogs.

“We have remained in regular contact with neighbours and will continue to offer support and take all necessary steps to protect residents and restore stability to the area.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Sussex Police added: “Sussex Police will continue to assist Brighton and Hove City Council – as the lead agency – and will monitor and respond to any reported breaches.”

News.title: Large fire erupts at UK RAF base being used by US bombers including B-52s during Iran war
News.content:
A MAJOR fire has broken out at an RAF base where US bombers used in the offensive against Iran are housed.

An investigation has been started after one of the buildings at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire caught ablaze in the early hours of the morning.





A video shows a huge inferno, with flames engulfing the former commissary building on the perimeter of the base during the night.

It is understood the fire started in a disused building around 1am last night and no one was injured in the dramatic blaze.

The Ministry of Defence confirmed no RAF personnel were involved in the firefighting activities.

Photos show dozens of fire service personnel responding to the blaze at the RAF base, recently the target of anti-war protests.



The US Air Force confirmed there is an ongoing investigation into the circumstances of the fire, with any further updates to be released.

Crews from Gloucestershire and Oxfordshire Fire Services attended the scene, as well as ambulance crews and National Inter-Agency Liaison Officers.

Pictures from the scene show a large articulated arm spraying water down from its platform onto the roof of the building.

Fairford is a key European operations centre for the US Air Force, often used to house bombers.



In recent weeks, locals have complained of the disruption caused by the loud planes and an influx of planespotters to their quaint Cotwolds villages.

It has also been the site of recent protests against the war and Keir Starmer‘s U-turn decision to allow the US to use British bases to launch strikes on Iran.

The Gloucestershire base has become the target of recent protests in light of the US use of UK bases to launch attacks on Iran.

Around 200 people gathered yesterday for a demonstration in Fairfield.

The anti-war campaigners chanted “hands off Iran“, marching to the end of the base’s two-mile runway.



Surrounding roads were closed and residents told to expect disruption, but no arrests were made.

A US Air Force spokesperson confirmed: “There were no injuries sustained, the fire has been contained and currently poses no risk to the base populus or local community.

“We are thankful for the support of our local community members and services, the safety of our personnel, families, and surrounding communities remains our top priority.

“An investigation has been initiated and is ongoing, more information will be released as it becomes available.”

News.title: Popular HiPP baby food is urgently recalled from all shops over serious health risk as parents warned ‘do not eat’
News.content:
TOT FEARS Popular HiPP baby food is urgently recalled from all shops over serious health risk as parents warned ‘do not eat’

Credit: Getty

A POPULAR baby food has been urgently recalled over a serious health risk.

The product, sold at all major UK supermarkets, are being returned after the jars were mislabelled.





HiPP Organic Vegetable Lasagne did not list celeriac, an allergen, in bold on its ingredients list.

The statement from the Food Standards Agency (FSA) recall notice read: “This product contains celeriac making it a possible health risk for anyone with an allergy to celery.”

Celery is one of the 14 main allergens which food producers must flag on their ingredients list – in bold, underlined or using contrasting colours.

According to Allergy UK, celery allergies can have mild symptoms like itchy mouth, lips and throat.



But primary celery allergy can have more severe reactions, including potentially fatal anaphylaxis.

Baby food company HiPP recalled the 7+ months 190g Vegetable Lasagne jar due to the mistake.

Their recall notice explained this was “due to a labelling error which occurred during the latest artwork print refresh”.

“The allergen celeriac has not been highlighted in bold within the ingredients list, which makes it a possible health risk for babies with an allergy to celeriac.”



Affected jars are associated with the batch code B49311 and a best before end date of 31.1.2027.

Customers with affected jars in their cupboards have been urged not to feed it to their baby if they have an allergy to celery or celeriac.

Parents in this position are urged to contact HiPP for reimbursement.

The brand has stressed there are no other HiPP Organic products affected by the recall.

But the health risk fears come just days after rat poison was found inside a jar of HiPP baby food in Austria.



The shocking discovery came after the product was recalled from 1,500 over supermarket fears.

A sample from one of the recalled jars of “Carrots and Potatoes” baby food tested positive for rat poison, police in Burgenland, Austria, said.

HiPP said the jars may have been tampered with.

It could not be ruled out that a dangerous substance was introduced into the product, the company said.

HiPP said: “According to our current knowledge, this critical situation involves an external criminal interference that affects the SPAR Austria distribution channel.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Austria’s agency for food protection said the poison may have been introduced as part of an extortion scheme.

A SPAR spokesperson said the product recall was a precautionary measure affecting 1,500 stores in Austria, with no impact on outlets elsewhere.

News.title: Three pedestrians injured after fire engine crashes with car before hitting building – as man in his 30s arrested
News.content:
CRASH ARREST Three pedestrians injured after fire engine crashes with car before hitting building – as man in his 30s arrested

THREE pedestrians have been injured after a fire engine crashed with a car before slamming into a building.

The vehicles collided on Sidbury in Worcester at around 6pm – bringing the city centre to a standstill with emergency services rushing to the scene.



A man in his 30s has been arrested on suspicion of causing serious injury by careless driving after he drove into the fire engine.

The vehicles collided on Sidbury in Worcester at around 6PM bringing the city centre to a stand still with emergency services rushing to the scene.



The crash caused the firetruck to slam into a nearby building with the suspect remaining in custody for questioning.

West Mercia Police said: “Three pedestrians were injured today (April 25) following a two-vehicle collision in Worcester city centre.

“Officers were called to Sidbury around 6pm after a fire engine and a car collided. The fire engine then collided with a building.

“Two pedestrians suffered serious injuries as a result of the collision, and a third pedestrian suffered minor injuries.



“A man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of causing serious injury by careless driving. He remains in police custody as enquiries continue.”

An air ambulance was sent to the scene and was spotted heading in the direction of Birmingham.

Around the same time, an overturned car was spotted on nearby Bullring Roundabout in St John’s but it is unclear whether the incidents are related.

News.title: One blast away from millions dead, Soviet cover-ups & secret files – Chernobyl nuclear disaster laid bare 40 years on
News.content:
IN the dead of night 40 years ago on April 26, 1986, nothing seemed out of the ordinary at the now abandoned Chernobyl nuclear power plant.

Engineers were carrying out safety tests on Reactor 4 – unaware that the world’s worst nuclear disaster was about to unfold, releasing 400 times more radiation than the Hiroshima atomic bomb.





The operators working on the reactor had been testing whether it could still be cooled during a power blackout. They had disabled critical safety systems and everything was going to plan.

But at around 1.23am, a dramatic power surge sparked an explosion as the reactor lost coolant.

The blast blew off the reactor’s lid – leaving the core exposed and spewing out radioactive material equivalent to 500 nuclear bombs.

It was followed by a huge blaze that continued to burn for days after the first explosion, sending radioactive particles billowing into the sky and across Europe and the Soviet Union.



Emergency responders, firefighters and plant workers scrambled to the scene – unaware of the extreme radiation levels surging through the air around them.

Dozens of workers suffered radiation sickness, some later dying from their exposure to the toxic waves.

Nearby, the city of Pripyat was not evacuated until 36 hours after the first explosion, leaving tens of thousands of people exposed to radiation.

Rain dumped the radioactive material as far as 1,800 miles away in Wales, leading to a ban on selling lamb which had grazed the contaminated land as it was not safe for people to eat.



It’s estimated up to five million people were exposed to extreme radiation across Belarus, Ukraine and Russia.

In the immediate aftermath 31 people died – including two at the scene and 29 firefighters – but radiation poisoning means the long-term death toll could be as high as 500,000.

But the accident in 1986 could have been even more catastrophic were it not for three heroic volunteers who selflessly risked their own lives to prevent a further explosion.

Days after the explosion, authorities discovered the core of the exploded reactor was still melting down.

Underneath this was a huge pool of water, which acted as a coolant for the power plant.



And the melting core was nearing the water – which, had they mixed, would have caused a second steam explosion.

Estimates suggest that had this been allowed to happen, half of Europe would have been wiped out, many millions would have perished, and the entire area would have been uninhabitable for over 500,000 years.



Soviet physicist Vassili Nesterenko said: “Minsk, which is 320 kilometres from Chernobyl, would have been razed and Europe rendered uninhabitable.”

Firefighters had tried, unsuccessfully, to fully drain the pool containing 20 million litres of water using specialised hoses.

A team of three volunteers stepped in to go down to the water tank and open a valve to release the water, described as “like finding a needle in a haystack”.

Two plant engineers, Alexei Ananenko and Valeri Bezpalov and shift supervisor Boris Baranov, were told they could refuse the assignment – which became known as a “suicide mission”.

But the heroic men went into the basement wearing wetsuits and had the radioactive water up to their knees.



Contrary to reports that all three died from poisoning within weeks, the men survived their mission and risked their lives to save millions.

Without them, an additional 77 square miles would have been destroyed, and the water supply for 30 million people and northern Ukraine would have been unusable for more than a century.

In the aftermath of the disaster, the Soviet government – headed up by Mikhail Gorbachev – attempted to cover up the disaster.

But it soon became an impossible feat as increased radiation levels were recorded across European cities.

Documents on the extent of radiation exposure only came to light after the reunification of Germany in 1991, following the fall of the Berlin Wall two years earlier.



Formerly top secret Soviet files showed that while Gorbachev was publicly insisting the situation was under control, top officials knew how far-reaching the explosion had actually been.

In the damning document, The Secret Chernobyl Documents, Gorbachev said: “When we inform the public, we should say that the power plant was being renovated at the time, so it doesn’t reflect badly on our reactor equipment.”



A 1991 investigation accused Communist leaders at the time of a “massive criminal cover-up that led to thousands of deaths”.

A commission laid bare the efforts the regime had gone to in order to portray a vision of normalcy to the outside world and their own people.

One shocking note found that in Pripyat, weddings were ordered to go ahead on the day of the accident despite a shower of radioactivity, to persuade people that nothing was amiss.

The commission chairman, Volodymyr Yavorivsky, said “everyone in the upper echelons of power knew everything” less than 12 hours after the explosion.

The revelations showed how the Soviet administration was willing to not just lie to the outside world – but also to their own people.



In the weeks after the disaster, traces of radioactive deposits were found in Belarus, where poisonous rain damaged plants and caused animal mutations.

The devastating impact was also felt in Scandinavia, Switzerland, Greece, Italy, France and the UK.

The World Health Organisation reported that food chains across Europe were impacted due to radiation waves – affecting fish in Germany and Scandinavia.

Toxic chemicals were also found in game, berries and mushrooms in other parts of Europe.

Eventually, a massive containment effort was launched, with hundreds of thousands of liquidators sent to clean up the radioactive debris.



The liquidators worked to extinguish fires and construct a concrete sarcophagus to contain the damaged reactor.

More than 650,000 frontline soldiers, firefighters and civilians helped to clean up Chernobyl over a four-year period after the nuclear meltdown.

Petro Hurin, 76, was one of those liquidators.



He and 39 other workers were sent into the Ukrainian nuclear plant just a month after the explosion.

Four decades on, Petro said his health has never been the same.

One of five last surviving liquidators of that group, he said not a single worker who had been deployed into the radiation-affected zone was in good health again, describing it as “death by a thousand cuts”.

New information about the devastating explosion continues to reveal the long-lasting effects as survivors like Petro tell harrowing stories of death and heartbreak.

Russian scientists estimate up to 125,000 volunteers had died by 2005, although authorities still deny a definitive link between the fatality rate and radiation exposure.



Working gruelling 12-hour shifts, Petro used an excavator to load dry concrete mixed with lead — shipped to the site by river barge — onto trucks for transport to the plant.

The lead-laced concrete was then used to make the sarcophagus encasement sealing in the exploded reactor.

After just four days, Petro said he was experiencing symptoms including headaches, chest pain, bleeding, and had a constant metallic taste in his throat.

Soviet doctors refused to diagnose him with radiation sickness, a finding that was not permitted at the time.



In 2000, the last of Chernobyl’s reactors was decommissioned and the Zone Of Alienation around the plant became a ­macabre tourist destination.

A 1,000-square-mile zone was cordoned off to prevent harmful exposure to people, with only about 1,000 residents having returned to the exclusion zone, now part of Ukraine, in the four decades since they left.

Humans inhabiting the area and the nearby town of Pripyat – which was built to serve the plant and house workers – had fled after finding the explosion had resulted in the spread of cancer-causing radiation.

Since then, plants and animals, including packs of wolves, grizzly bears, bison, and elk, have reclaimed the site of the nuclear disaster, some of which seem unaffected by the high levels of radiation.

But lingering health impacts from the radiation exposure have trickled through generations, with many children of the liquidators suffering the consequences.



Researchers in 2025 revealed that DNA mutations have been detected in the children of those originally exposed to the disaster.

Increased rates of thyroid cancer – particularly in people exposed to the radiation as children – have also been a long-term health impact of the explosion.



And children of workers haven’t been the only ones affected by the toxic matter contaminating the environment.

It was reported that the radioactive ruins of the nuclear plant have turned several stray dogs blue.

Footage shared last year by organisation Dogs of Chernobyl shows three blue-tinted hounds roaming free near the infamous power plant.

A spokesperson said: “We’ve seen a lot in Chernobyl, but this was a very unique experience. We are not sure exactly what is going on.

“We do not know the reason, and we are attempting to catch them so we can find out what is happening. Most likely, they’re getting into some sort of chemical.”



The dogs have been seen roaming large areas of contaminated land in Ukraine, Belarus and Russia.

Wild wolves also wander the nuclear wilderness near Chernobyl – with researchers suggesting they may have developed a “superpower” after prolonged exposure to radiation.

Scientists are hoping their discovery of the genetic mutation could give humans a better chance of surviving cancer.

Today, the risk of another nuclear disaster is rising as Russia’s invasion of Ukraine rages on for a fourth year – with Putin’s military spotted flying as many as 35 missiles over the abandoned plant.

General Ruslan Kravchenko revealed unreported Russian activity near the site – ahead of Ukraine marking the 40th anniversary of the disaster.



Alongside Chernobyl, Ukraine is home to four other nuclear power plants, including Zaporizhzhia — Europe’s largest – which has been under Russian control since the start of the invasion in 2022.

Chernobyl and the Khmelnytskyi nuclear plant in western Ukraine have been on the flight path of Russian missiles, according to Kravchenko.

The International Atomic Energy Agency said it has “deep concern” about military activity in the vicinity of nuclear power plants today.

News.title: Trump stumbles in dramatic footage as he's helped from dinner shooting scene
News.content:
Trump stumbles in dramatic footage as he's helped from dinner shooting scene

Footage showed Trump being helped by security and secret service agents as he appeared to fall while being rushed off the stage during the shooting at the White House Correspondents' Dinner

Trump and JD Vance evacuated from dinner after gunshot

Donald Trump was filmed appearing to stumble as he was helped off the stage by special agents after a gunman opened fire during the Wh ite House Correspondents' Dinner.

‌



Cole Tomas Allen, 31, from Torrance, California, has been identified as the suspected gunman who was armed with guns and knives when he stormed the Washington Hilton on Saturday night.

‌



As chaos broke out in the room, the president was rushed off the stage along with the other guests.

‌



Vice President JD Vance was removed from the room first, while agents initially covered Donald Trump with automatic weapons before escorting him and First Lady Melania Trump away.

Footage appears to show Trump stumbling on his way offstage as he was assisted by security and secret service agents.

News.title: Concerns for King's safety top priority after Donald Trump shooting chaos at White House event
News.content:
Concerns for King's safety top priority after Donald Trump shooting chaos at White House event

The bedlam that ensued in what appears to be another assassination attempt on President Donald Trump will prompt major talks on security for King Charles' US visit

View 4 Images Charles' safety has been thrown into sharp focus ahead of his next meeting with Donald Trump (Image: AP)

The distressing scenes witnessed in Washington and a city under lockdown will be a grave concern for those planning the King and Queen's upcoming visit to the United States.

‌



Hundreds of police officers descended on the capital from all directions last night, as the already huge security operation at the Hilton hotel in the capital went into overdrive. Already in Washington ahead of the royals’ arrival, I was just a mile away with Mirror photographer Ian Vogler walking back from dinner when the chaos erupted.

‌



Police sirens blasted and cars screeched around the corner, clearly signifying a serious incident was unfolding. Just moments before, at 8.36pm, a lone man armed with a shotgun, a handgun and multiple knives breached a checkpoint in the hotel lobby and sprinted toward the ballroom where the glittering event attended by the US President, the First Lady, Vice President and several members of the cabinet, as well as hundreds of political journalists, was about to begin.

‌



View 4 Images The top table - with the president and first lady - react in shock as shots ring out (Image: BBC)

A colleague who was trapped inside the hotel texted me within minutes to relay the chaos of the unfolding situation as the Secret Service personnel stormed the event and rushed the President and his top team out of harm's way. The assailant was brought down and taken into custody after firing off several shots, including at one agent who was saved by his bullet proof vest.

President Trump’s willingness at first to continue with the planned evening, despite yet another clear threat to his life, speaks to the nature of how some Americans view gun violence as a way of life. But serious questions will have to be asked as to how a heavily armed attacker could have breached security at such a high profile event.

‌



View 4 Images Mirror Royal Editor Russell Myers reporting near the White House hours before the shooting

Security was already of paramount importance for the King and Queen’s visit to the US and will no doubt be completely reviewed in light of the terrifying situation last night.

Buckingham Palace and royal protection teams will be seeking assurances that a watertight operation will be in place ahead of the royal visit, something that appears to not be guaranteed at any stage in a country with such shocking gun violence statistics.

‌



Royal sources said the King and Queen has reached out privately to The President and First Lady to express their sympathies with all those affected on the night and their gratitude to the security services who prevented further injury.

View 4 Images Cole Tomas Allen has been arrested as the shooting suspect (Image: TRUTH SOCIAL)

The State Visit has been hit with controversy for a number of reasons, further to the decision by the British government asking the King and Queen to travel to the US, amid Trump's war against Iran and continued brutal comments aimed at the Prime Minister for not joining in the conflict.

Article continues below

Yet concerns over the King and Queen’s safety will now be of paramount importance, adding another layer of stress to this already high profile occasion.

A Buckingham Palace spokesman said: "His Majesty is being kept fully informed of developments and is greatly relieved to hear that the President, First Lady and all guests have been unharmed.

"As you would expect, a number of discussions will be taking place throughout the day to discuss with US colleagues and our respective teams to what degree the events of Saturday evening may or may not impact on the operational planning for the Visit."

News.title: ‘I live in other people’s homes and don’t pay rent after horrible house shares’
News.content:
‘I live in other people’s homes and don’t pay rent after horrible house shares’

A 25-year-old has given up living in her own space thanks to her new profession but admits it has some downsides

View 3 Images Tara Little has no plans to get a permanent address any time soon (Image: Jam Press/@little_tarz)

Tara Little was struggling with rent payments, finding work and “horrible” housing situations when she discovered a simple career change that fixed it all for her. But she admits the lifestyle isn’t for everyone and has some major downsides.

‌



The 25-year-old has become a full-time housesitter, living in other people’s homes year-round. The mutually beneficial partnership gives Tara some income and a place to live while the homeowners get peace of mind that their property and pets are taken care of when they are away.

‌



Thanks to her new occupation, Tara has been able to stay in almost every suburb of her native Darwin, Australia. Paired with her other work as a social media manager, Tara is living her dream as she gets to save money, avoid roommates and spend her days with adorable pets.

‌



She told creatorzine.com : “The best part of house-sitting is being able to live in solitude and without the stress of paying rent or bills. No waking up to housemates slamming doors or clanging kitchen pots, and no bickering over who left their dirty dishes in the sink!

“On top of this, I enjoy beautiful homes, spend time with adorable animals, and most importantly, I save money.

“I have had some horrible past experiences living in shared houses, and am so grateful that house-sitting has given me the opportunity to live independently.”

‌



View 3 Images Tara has been able to stay at some stunning and remote properties (Image: Jam Press/@little_tarz)

The 25-year-old explained that she sets her own daily rate for housesitting and finds regular clients through two main platforms or Facebook groups. She’ll then set up meetings with the homeowners to go over the layout of the house, routines, pets and exchange keys.

Each house has different rules and Tara revealed this lifestyle may not be a great match for everyone. In some cases she has been limited on when she can leave the house due to anxious pets and one of the most common rules she has to live with is not hosting any parties.

‌



She can also only bring a limited amount of luggage with her. Tara shared: “Living out of three suitcases is the biggest challenge I face as a house-sitter, especially as someone who loves fashion and trinkets.

“I’ve had to learn to minimise my wardrobe and stop indulging in buying useless things. House-sitting has shown me how much we all participate in overconsumption and has forced me to make better choices in spending.

“Because of my lifestyle as a house-sitter, there's honestly not much I can buy. I can no longer indulge in buying things that I used to, like clothes and trinkets, because I don't have a home of my own to store them.”

‌



Tara estimates she’s saved around $10,000AUD (£5,298) a year in rent and bills alone thanks to her housesitting lifestyle. Although she has only earned around $5,000 from house-sitting over the past year, Tara revealed that taking away the stress of paying all of her rent and bills allowed her to focus more on building her social media business.

She continued: “My second biggest trial as a house-sitter has been the moving process.

“I have thankfully gotten used to it, but some days are still a challenge; the last days of a house-sit are the hardest because it usually involves the most tedious and painful tasks- cleaning the house, packing the suitcases and loading the car.”

‌



View 3 Images Tara often has to follow specific rules for each house and pet she looks after (Image: Jam Press/@little_tarz)

Tara has also faced a few cancellations, which can be extra nerve-wracking when she’s relying on bookings for a place to live. She said: “It can be difficult to secure a new house-sit when cancellations occur, especially at the last minute! I’m lucky I have amazing family and friends living in Darwin that are happy to take me in when this happens!”

Tara has no plans to settle down to a permanent address. In fact, she hopes her future holds a van that she can travel across Australia with.

Article continues below

She said: “I would love to take care of people’s pets and homes when and where I can find house-sitting opportunities, and stay in my van in between house-sits. This is my dream.

“I’ve definitely gained much more from my lifestyle as a house-sitter. The only loss is the comfort of living in one place.”

News.title: Trump security incidents including assassination attempt and 'ricin poisoning' after shooting
News.content:
Trump security incidents including assassination attempt and 'ricin poisoning' after shooting

Chaos ensued after a gunman opened fire at the White House correspondents' dinner last night, but it is the latest in a long line of security incidents involving US President Donald Trump

View 5 Images Donald Trump after the assassination attempt in Pennsylvania (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

US President Donald Trump has been the subject of another apparent attack as gunshots sparked chaos at the White House correspondents' dinner last night (Saturday, April 25).

‌



On the eve of King Charles' and Camilla's state visit to the USA, Trump and his wife Melania were evacuated from the event at the Washington Hilton after gunfire rang out.

‌



The President has suffered a number of assassination attempts during his time in the White House, both during his first time from January 2017 to January 2021. He was also targeted while running for a second term and since his re-election.

‌



From an attempted shooting at a Pennsylvania rally to apparent ricin poisoning attempts, below are some of the major security incidents involving Trump.

View 5 Images The Secret Service arrested the suspect (Image: Getty Images)

Dinner shooting

Trump and his wife were among those evacuated from the White House correspondents' dinner last night, along with Vice President JD Vance and other members of the Cabinet.

‌



Hundreds of guests hid under tables in the ballroom as US Secret Service rushed in shouting 'shots fired'. One Secret Service agent was reportedly shot at very close range but was saved by his bullet proof vest.

The shooting suspect was identified as Cole Tomas Allen, 31, of Torrance, California, according to multiple news outlets. He is expected to be formally charged tomorrow (Monday). He had apparently sneaked into the venue as a guest.

Police added that the suspect was armed with multiple weapons, including a shotgun, handgun and knives.

‌



View 5 Images Trump was defiant after the Pennsylvania rally shooting (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Pennsylvania rally attack

Trump was seriously injured when he was shot while speaking at a rally in Pennsylvania in July 2024. Trump was shot and wounded in his upper right ear by 20-year-old Thomas Crooks as he campaigned as the Republican Party's nominee for the 2024 election.

Crooks fired eight rounds from an AR-15-style rifle from a nearby building's roof at the open-air rally near the city of Butler.

‌



He also killed an audience member, Corey Comperatore, and critically injured two others. Crooks was shot and killed by the Secret Service within seconds.

Secret Service agents shielded Trump until the shooter had been killed. A photojournalist captured the then ex-President with blood on his face and ear, pumping his fist in the air while saying "Fight! Fight! Fight."

Trump made his first public appearance since the assassination attempt two days later at the 2024 Republic National Convention in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, with a bandage on his ear.

‌



The incident is regarded as the Secret Service's most significant security failure since the attempted assassination of President Ronald Reagan in 1981. Coincidentally, the Reagan incident happened at the same venue as last night's shooting at the correspondents' dinner.

View 5 Images A man attempted to kill Trump at one of his golf clubs (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Trump Golf Club incident

Just two months after the assassination attempt in Pennsylvania, Trump was subjected to another attempt on his life.

‌



Ryan Wesley Routh, who had been planning an attack for months, was spotted hiding in shrubbery near the Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach, Florida, on September 15, 2024. He was holding an SKS rifle and had been there for 12 hours.

Routh pointed his weapon through the fence line, approximately 370m away from Trump.

A Secret Service agent fired four rounds towards Routh, who fled the scene and was later captured in nearby Martin County through a traffic stop. A six-year-old girl, Mia Rosalie Monreal, received life-threatening injuries following a car crash caused by the traffic stop.

‌



Routh was found guilty on five federal counts, including attempting to assassinate a presidential candidate. In February this year he was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole plus seven years.

View 5 Images A British man said he planned to kill Trump in Las Vegas (Image: AFP/Getty Images)

Las Vegas rally assassination attempt

While Trump was campaigning to be elected for the first time, Michael Steven Sandford attempted to grab the pistol of a Las Vegas Metropolitan Police officer during an event in the city.

‌



Sandford, a 20-year-old British citizen, failed in his bid and was arrested at the rally on June 18, 2016. He claimed that he had wished to kill Trump to stop him being elected U.S president.

He was charged with disorderly conduct and with being an illegal alien in possession of a firearm. He pleaded guilty to both charges and was sentenced to 12 months and one day of imprisonment. Sandford was released and deported to the UK after 11 months in custody.

Trump briefly acknowledged the incident in his campaign speech, saying: "We love you, police. Thank you. Thank you, officers." The attempt received little coverage in the American media, with journalists and political commentators suggesting this was due to its "feebly unsophisticated" and "poorly conceived nature".

‌



They also suggested that the suspect's status as a "white British non-Muslim man did not fit his narrative of a threat".

'Ricin' poisoning attempts

Trump has twice been the victim of apparent ricin poisoning attempts. On October 1, 2018, an envelope containing castor beans was sent to the President before being discovered by mailing facilities.

It was initially incorrectly identified as ricin. Several other letters were sent to the Pentagon all of them labelled with 'Jack and the Missile Bean Stock Powder'. Navy veteran William Clyde Allen III was arrested and charged with one count of mailing a threat against the president and five counts of mailing threatening communications to an officer or an employee of the United States.

‌



Allen pleaded not guilty to all charges. He was remanded for psychiatric evaluation and treatment before the charges against him were dismissed on January 25, 2022.

On September 20, 2020, Pascale Cécile Véronique Ferrier was arrested in Buffalo, New York, while attempting to cross the border into Canada. He wrote a ricin-laced letter to Trump calling him for to drop out of the 2020 presidential election. He also called him an "ugly tyrant clown".

She was charged with eight counts each of prohibitions with respect to biological weapons and making threats via interstate commerce and faced up to life in prison. She was sentenced to nearly 22 years in prison on August 17, 2023.

Article continues below

On September 20, 2020, Pascale Cécile Véronique Ferrier was arrested in Buffalo, New York, while attempting to cross over the border to Canada. Ferrier, who is Canadian, wrote in a ricin-laced letter to Trump that he should drop out of the ongoing 2020 presidential election along with calling him an "ugly tyrant clown". She was charged with eight counts each of prohibitions with respect to biological weapons and making threats via interstate commerce and faced up to life in prison.[10][11] On August 17, 2023, a US court sentenced Ferrier to nearly 22 years in prison

News.title: Brits face higher prices for eight months after Iran war ends, warns top minister
News.content:
Brits face higher prices for eight months after Iran war ends, warns top minister

Darren Jones, the Chief Secretary to the Prime Minister, delivered a grim verdict on the economic hit from the Iran war as the Government steps up planning to shield Brits

View 2 Images The economic impact of the Iran war will be felt by Brits for months (Image: PA)

People in the UK could face higher costs for food, energy and flights for at least eight months after the Iran war ends, a top minister has warned.

‌



Darren Jones, the Chief Secretary to the Prime Minister, delivered the grim verdict on the economic hit from the US-Israeli conflict with Iran as the Government steps up planning to shield Brits from being clobbered.

‌



Tehran's effective blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has caused energy prices to rocket around the world, and ministers have carried out worst-case scenario planning for food shortages this summer.

‌



Mr Jones said “price pressure” was more likely than shortages on supermarket shelves during an interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme. He said: “You’re going to see prices go up a bit as a consequence of what Donald Trump has done in the Middle East.

UK steps up plans for potential food and fuel shortages triggered by Iran war READ MORE :

King's security for US state visit under scrutiny as shots fired at Trump dinner READ MORE :

View 2 Images Top minister Darren Jones issued a grim warning about the economic hit from the Iran war (Image: Jeff Overs/BBC/PA Wire)

"And quite frankly, that’s probably going to come online, not just in the next few weeks, but the next few months. There’s going to be a long tail from this."

‌



Asked how long higher prices – such as for petrol and diesel – might remain, he said: “I think our best guess is eight-plus months from the point of resolution that you’ll see economic impacts coming through the system.”

He added: “People will see higher energy prices, food prices and those types of issues, flight ticket prices, as a consequence of what Donald Trump has done in the Middle East.

“The Government here in the UK, the work that I’m doing with the Prime Minister is looking at all of those things and saying, ‘What can we do within our power to help people to get through those difficult times?'”

‌



Keir Starmer is expected to chair another meeting of the crisis committee set up to deal with shortfalls on Tuesday. A contingency planning group of ministers led by Mr Jones to monitor supply chains and stock levels is also meeting twice a week.

The Government is working to ensure pubs don't run out of beer during the World Cup, he said.

Asked if there was a beer committee to ensure there are no shortages if supplies of carbon dioxide run low, Mr Jones said: “I raised this issue because if there is a problem with jet fuel on holidays and carbon dioxide on beer the summer might be pretty depressing for people, but we’re doing everything we can to make sure that it’s not the case.”

Article continues below

Meanwhile, ministers are drawing up plans to make it easier for airlines to cancel flights without running the risk of losing their allocated slots if fuel shortages prevent them from flying.

Supermarkets are also working with the Government to plan for a worst-case scenario of shortages of carbon dioxide, which is used in the slaughter of some animals and in food preservation.

News.title: Best electrolyte powders for rehydration– and how much London Marathon runners need
News.content:
Best electrolyte powders for rehydration– and how much London Marathon runners need

With searches for electrolytes at an all-time high, we look at who needs the hydration boost and what happens if you don’t

View 3 Images Most of us actually get enough electrolytes from everyday foods – but that's not the case for marathon runners (Image: Getty)

Electrolytes are officially having a moment – especially this week with the marathon happening in sunny London. The global electrolyte drink market is worth over £30 billion and growing 5–6% a year, thanks to people chasing better daily wellness and clever marketing from sports drink brands. And for the most part, there’s a real reason behind the hype: even losing just 1–2% of your body weight in water can slow your focus and reaction time. Experts agree that beating brain fog starts with staying properly hydrated.

So, if you’ve been in runner training and reaching for a sachet of electrolytes daily, you may assume you’re doing the best thing for your body. After all, they’re the minerals– think sodium, potassium, magnesium and calcium– that keep your body working. They also help your nerves fire, your muscles flex and your heart beat like it’s supposed to.

But the thing is, most of us actually get enough from everyday foods like bananas, leafy greens, dairy, nuts and even dark chocolate, so by supplementing electrolytes daily, you might be overloading your body (more on this in a moment).

There are, however, some exceptions to this. If you’ve been sweating buckets (heavy exercise or from hot temperatures – ie, if you're training for a marathon), battling a bug or skipping water for hours, your levels can dip, and things like fatigue, cramps and nausea can set in. When this happens, electrolytes can be just the trick to support your body.



View 3 Images Electrolytes are officially having a moment – but not everyone needs them (Image: Getty)

If your current state doesn’t fall into these categories, a little caution is worth keeping in mind. According to Heart.org, excess sodium can raise blood pressure, and most Brits are already eating way too much. Guidelines recommend adults stick to no more than about one teaspoon a day. Yet the average intake is 1.5 teaspoons without the help of electrolytes.

Essentially, your body is pretty good at balancing electrolytes on its own, filtering the excess through urine, but too much sodium from foods or supplements can tip the scales. So while a little extra electrolytes can help in the right situations, more isn’t always better.

But what about the electrolyte drinks and powders that say ‘for daily use’ on their labels, you ask? These are typically formulated with lower, balanced doses of electrolytes, rather than targeted at athletes who might require higher doses. So if you aren’t a heavy exerciser, these daily sachets are your best bet if you do feel like you need a little electrolyte kick.

Best electrolyte powders, according to a shopping expert

Our Shopping Lead Zoe turns to electrolytes after sweaty workouts – these are the ones she says are the best tasting

View 3 Images Zoe shares three of her favourite electrolyte powders (Image: Zoe Cripps)

O.R.S Hydration for Sports, £7.99 for 20

Zoe says: ‘I reach for these on days I do long cycle classes or boxing workouts. I have a tendency to get dehydrated easily, so these are great when I really need a boost. I like how affordable they are compared to other brands, and the taste is fine (the berry flavour is the best, in my opinion). They aren’t my favourite, but a good gym bag addition.”

Zoe says: “Now this is my absolute favourite. The apricot flavour was so popular when it launched as a limited edition the other summer that the brand has since made it a permanent option on the website. Many electrolyte powders have an unpleasant aftertaste or an overly salty or sweet tang, but Humantra is by far the most drinkable. I even enjoy drinking it. The only problem is that a box of 20 is a little pricey, so I don’t buy it every month.”

Article continues below

Four Five Plus+ Hydro Plus Everyday Recovery, £33 (currently £22) for 30 Sachets

Zoe says: “When I see this on sale at Holland & Barrett, I always grab a box because it’s my daily pick. I understand the guidance on electrolytes, but I am very active, and I suffer from migraines, so I’ve really found that keeping my hydration up helps keep them at bay. I don’t supplement on days when I don’t work out, but when I feel even a little dehydrated, I always have a sachet of Four Five+ in my cupboard. If you can find the tart cherry flavour, it’s definitely the tastiest.”

News.title: Abandoned graveyard shame as 9,000 psychiatric patients forgotten - Titanic survivor to Picasso muse
News.content:
Abandoned graveyard shame as 9,000 psychiatric patients forgotten - Titanic survivor to Picasso muse

9000 former psychiatric patients are buried at Horton Cemetery in London. A campaign aims to bring the site back into public ownership and preserve the memory of those buried there

View 7 Images Felicja Staszewicz - a member of the Polish nobility who is buried at Horton Cemetery

Overgrown and unloved, around 9,000 former patients of what was once the largest cluster of psychiatric hospitals in Europe are buried at Horton Cemetery in Surrey. Lost souls, they come from all walks of life and include a Titanic survivor, a Polish noblewoman and even a muse of Picasso. Now a major campaign is underway to bring the privately owned five acre site back into public ownership and preserve the memory of those buried there.

‌



Lionel Blackman, honorary secretary of the charity Friends of Horton Cemetery, which is spearheading the drive, says: “We think Horton is of national importance. We believe it is the largest abandoned hospital cemetery in Europe. That makes it a rich resource for historians. The more stories we uncover of the people who are buried there, the better we can understand their lives and society at the time.”

‌



Lionel, a lawyer from Surrey, also believes the stories of Horton’s lost souls may help banish the stigma towards mental illness today. He says: “These were people just like me and you - butchers, hat makers, piano tuners - but they fell into poverty or became ill and came to an unfortunate end.”

‌



View 7 Images Mary Ann Godfrey - a patient at Horton

Once back in public ownership, the charity wants to see the site become a garden, nature reserve and memorial to those buried there - information on around 500 of whom has been found by its volunteer researchers. Meanwhile, a granite memorial outside the cemetery, paid for by public subscription, is the only indicator of its past.

The Epsom cluster was a group of five large psychiatric hospitals built by the London County Council. The Manor, Horton, Ewell Epileptic Colony, Long Grove and West Park asylums began operation in 1899, offering those suffering with mental illness an opportunity to recover in the fresh air of the countryside.

‌



But some of the reasons for committing people to asylums were truly shocking. Lionel says: “Trauma after miscarriage, for example. Remember, there was a time when a man could decide to have his wife certified. We have anecdotal evidence about women who had children out of wedlock ending up in psychiatric hospitals, while soldiers with shell shock might also be admitted.

And, of course, there is now no such thing as an ‘epileptic colony’ as there was on site at Horton - thank goodness. If family finances were strained, or no relatives came forward, those who died there between 1899 and 1955 were laid to rest in paupers’ graves on land at the heart of the estate”.

View 7 Images Alex Buchinger of Surbiton. He is a relative of Felicja Staszewicz, who is buried at Horton Cemetery.

‌



Few had headstones, most just a simple cross, although few of these remain. Felicja Staszewicz was a Polish noblewoman who entered the hospital site in 1947. A mother of ten, she was forced to flee her country estate at the outbreak of the Second World War. Arrested by invading Russian forces, she and her family worked as slave labourers, but were released in 1942.

Felicja arrived in the UK in 1947, but her health declined and she died at Horton in 1950. Her great grandson, Alex Buchinger, a semi-retired chartered engineer, from Surbiton, says: “We think she may have had dementia. I have huge admiration for her. She and the family lost everything - a noblewoman who ended up in a pauper’s grave. It would be lovely to be able to go and see her last resting place.”

Mary Ann Godfrey arrived at the Manor Hospital in 1912 and died three years later, aged 42, apparently suffering with ‘chronic melancholia’. “Today she would probably be diagnosed with anxiety and depression,” says Derek Andrews, 77, from Clacton-on-Sea. Mary Ann is his wife Patricia’s great grandmother. “We talk so much more about these things these days. There should be no shame”. Grateful that the charity preserves her memory, he is saddened by the dilapidated cemetery, saying: “It's more like a rubbish tip.”

‌



View 7 Images Long Grove Hospital, formerly Long Grove Asylum, was a mental hospital, part of the Epsom Cluster of hospitals in the Horton area of Epsom, Surrey in the United Kingdom.

Others buried at Horton include Manchester born Byron Pedley, a popular comedy actor and famed Spanish dancer Felix Garcia, who was sketched by Picasso. Burials at Horton stopped in 1955 and changes in the treatment of mental health patients in hospital meant numbers fell.

The hospitals were sold and in 1983 the Department of Health and Social Care sold the cemetery grounds to a local property investment firm. Lionel says: “Nothing has happened with it since. It’s mainly overgrown, largely impenetrable and protected only by an old iron fence. We would love to restore the cemetery to community ownership.”

‌



Epsom and Ewell Liberal Democrat MP, Helen Maguire, is backing the campaign. She says: "Horton Cemetery in my constituency remains a site of profound historical significance. It is the resting place of around 9,000 people, many of them among the most vulnerable in society, including former psychiatric patients, the poor, and those who in life had little voice or power.”

View 7 Images Aerial photographs of Horton Cemetery on the B284 near Epsom, Surrey. The overgrown patch of woodland is the final resting place of 9,000 forgotten mental health patients, piled in unmarked graves, sometimes three or four bodies deep. The dead include war heroes, a Titanic survivor, a famed Victorian actor, Picasso’s muse (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

Helen, who raised questions concerning Horton in the Commons, continues: "Horton is uniquely placed to serve as a pilot for any new legislation addressing neglected and abandoned burial grounds. It offers a real opportunity to lead the way in restoring dignity, proper memorialisation and long-term protection.”

‌



For Lionel, the quest to give Horton’s lost souls a dignified resting place, feels personal. He says: “Their stories never fail to move me and their tragedies often give me a chill down my spine. There is one about a boy soldier, Leslie Attwood, who lied about his age to join the military in 1914 - he was only 15. These people may have been born before all our time but in reality we’re not too distant from them.”

George Pelham

George Pelham survived the sinking of the Titanic in 1912 only to be torpedoed on another ship during WW1. It was perhaps because of these traumatic incidents that the London shoemaker’s son was admitted to Horton Psychiatric Hospital. A father to two boys when he went to sea, aged 38, family members believe an unhappy marriage to wife Elizabeth prompted the move.

View 7 Images George Pelham, a Titanic sinking survivor buried at Horton Cemetery

‌



The following year, in 1912, he was transferred to Titanic as a trimmer, responsible for moving coal from storage bunkers to the stokers. He survived Titanic and later years saw him working as a general labourer. By January 1935 he was admitted to Horton Psychiatric Hospital, after suffering a breakdown. He was moved in August 1939 to nearby Long Grove, where he died 42 days later.

Tottie Fay

‘Tottie Fay’ was dubbed ‘the worst and wickedest woman in London by a magistrate. From a poor background, she became a small-time thief and conwoman, using a variety of wealthy alter-egos and becoming something of a celebrity for doing so. Born in London in 1850, Tottie would claim to be an actress, or a lady of means; a governess, or newly arrived from the Continent - conning gentlemen out of cash and hoteliers out of food, drink and lodgings.

View 7 Images Tottie Fay, a Victorian conwoman buried at Horton Cemetery

Article continues below

An alcoholic, she was interned in various prisons and asylums, before being taken to Horton in 1902, discharged the following year, but readmitted in 1907. Even behind bars she fashioned costumes out of prison clothing and used brick dust and chalk as make-up. She died in 1908 aged 58. Her case was instrumental in pushing through The Inebriates Act of 1899, which championed reformative treatment rather than imprisonment for alcoholism.

News.title: Donald Trump suspect gunman member of student prank gun group that 'raid random buildings on campus and shoot'
News.content:
Donald Trump suspect gunman member of student prank gun group that 'raid random buildings on campus and shoot'

The suspected gunman who forced Donald Trump to evacuate from an event was part of a student prank group that would 'raid random buildings on campus'

Trump and JD Vance evacuated from dinner after gunshot

The suspected gunman who opened fire outside the White House correspondents' dinner, forcing Donald Trump to evacuate, was part of a student prank group who would "raid random buildings".

‌



Cole Tomas Allen, 31, was named as the suspect after shots were heard outside a ballroom holding 2,500 people - including Donald Trump, Melania Trump and JD Vance - for the annual dinner. The US President described the suspect as a "lone wolf whack job" after the incident around 8:35pm local time (01:35am UK time) on Saturday night, at the Washington Hilton hotel.

‌



The suspect was revealed to be a highly educated part-time teacher who was also a video game developer.

‌



View 5 Images Suspected White House correspondents' dinner shooter Cole Tomas Allen (Image: FACEBOOK)

King's security for US state visit under scrutiny as shots fired at Trump dinner READ MORE :

Allen graduated from the prestigious California Institute of Technology university in 2017 with a degree in mechanical engineering. His LinkedIn profile revealed the man had been a member of the university's Christian fellowship but also the NERF club.

NERF guns are toy weapons that fire soft darts, arrows and balls, which are often used by kids to play but sometimes popular with adults. Allen was part of the Caltech NERF group while a student, in the early 2010s.

‌



View 5 Images The moment the suspect was detained by police (Image: @REALDONALDTRUMP / TRUTH SOCIAL/AFP via Getty Images)

On Facebook, the uni group described itself as: "A group of people who raid random buildings on campus and shoot NERF guns at each other.

"Various other activities include: the modification of blasters for cool effects, mechanical improvements, and cosmetic bad-assery; shoot the Albert Yang game; long-term NERF games such as Red Vs Blue and Humans vs. Zombies."

‌



View 5 Images Stock image of several NERF gun toy weapons (Image: Gado via Getty Images)

Allen appeared to have been featured in a local news report, from 2017, as a Caltech student for developing a prototype emergency brake for wheelchairs. A spokesperson for the university said a person with the name Cole Allen had earned an undergraduate degree in 2017, according to the New York Times.

The man went on to later earn a Master of Science in Computer Science from a California State University-Dominguez Hills. A LinkedIn profile appearing to match the named suspect said he worked part-time as a teacher at a test prep and tutoring company, named C2 Education.

‌



View 5 Images Cole Tomas Allen (far right) in 2017 with his family

The company awarded the man "teacher of the month" in December 2024, according to social media posts. Allen also said he was a video game developer on his LinkedIn page and recently wrote he was "currently developing a second game, working name 'First Law.'" He published a game called Bohrdom and registered a trademark for the named back in 2018.

The US Attorney for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro, said the suspected is expected to appeared in court on Monday and be formally charged with several offences, including using a firearm during a crime of violence.

Article continues below

View 5 Images Authorities control suspect Cole Tomas Allen after the shooting (Image: AP)

This has been the third time since 2024 that the US President had been under threat by an attacker in his immediate vicinity – including the assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, that injured him and killed a local firefighter.

News.title: Watch: How gunfire sparked chaos at Trump press dinner
News.content:
US President Donald Trump had to be rushed to safety by his security agents after a gunman fired shots inside the hotel hosting the White House correspondents' dinner.

Others in attendance included Vice-President JD Vance, White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt, and a host of high-profile politicians, diplomats and journalists.

According to US media reports, the suspect has been identified as Cole Tomas Allen, 31, of Torrance, California.

Police said Allen was a guest at the Washington Hilton hotel, where the dinner was taking place, and was carrying multiple weapons - including guns and knives.

One US security agent was injured and received treatment in hospital, authorities said.

More on this story.

News.title: Sabastian Sawe smashes two-hour barrier to make history at London Marathon
News.content:
Sabastian Sawe made history at the London Marathon by becoming the first athlete to run a sub-two-hour marathon in a competitive race.

The 30-year-old Kenyan crossed the line to win in one hour 59 minutes 30 seconds, more than one minute faster than the late Kelvin Kiptum's previous record of 2:00:35, set in 2023.

The great Eliud Kipchoge became the first man to run a marathon in under two hours in 2019, but that was not record-eligible as it was held under controlled conditions.

Already on world record pace as he crossed the halfway mark in 1:00:29, Sawe was able to speed up over the second half of the race to run even faster than Kipchoge's time.

Sawe made his decisive move before the final 10km, with only debutant Yomif Kejelcha able to cover his surge off the front.

Remarkably, Kejelcha became the second man to run under two hours in race conditions, finishing runner-up in 1:59:41.

Half marathon world record holder Jacob Kiplimo also crossed the line faster than Kiptum's former record, completing the podium in 2:00:28.

Sawe, speaking on BBC TV, said: "I am feeling good. I am so happy. It is a day to remember for me."

Sabastian Sawe and Yomif Kejelcha made history by breaking the two-hour mark in a marathon for the first time in an astonishing London Marathon.

Champion Sawe obliterated the previous official world record with an astonishing run of 1:59:30. In an unbelievable twist, Kejelcha also broke the barrier with a time of 1:59:41.

The late Kelvin Kiptum previously held the world record with a time of 2:00:35 set in Chicago in 2023, with Eliud Kipchoge breaking the two-hour barrier in 2019, but not in official conditions.

In what will be remembered as the fastest marathon of all time, Jacob Kiplimo’s third-place time of 2:00:28 would have also broken the previous world record.

There was also a new women-only record set in the women’s race as Ethiopia’s Tigst Assefa defended her London Marathon crown with a time of 2:15:41.

Virgil van Dijk said he has no worries about the “outstanding” Alexander Isak despite his tough debut season at Liverpool and his lack of goals.

But the Liverpool captain said their record signing has to score more in the future after finally getting a Premier League goal at Anfield for Arne Slot’s side.

Isak, who cost a British record £125m, has only scored four goals in 21 games for Liverpool, three of them in the Premier League, in an injury-hit campaign.

Van Dijk said: “In terms of what I’ve seen of him everyone knows and sees and experiences as team-mates how outstanding he is. It is about getting games, confidence but obviously scoring goals as a striker – that’s the main trigger for him.

“I’m not worried at all about him whatsoever. We want more than goals from him and that’s what he can bring and he just has to keep going and keep working, keep staying fit and keep staying important for the football club because I think he will and he already is.”

Isak suffered a fractured leg when scoring against Tottenham in December and underwent ankle surgery. His goal in Saturday’s 3-1 win over Crystal Palace was his first in 2026.

Van Dijk hopes to see more goals from the former Newcastle player next season, though he is wary that his Netherlands side face Isak’s Sweden in Houston in June.

open image in gallery Alexander Isak scored his first goal of 2026 on Saturday against Crystal Palace ( Getty )

The defender added: “It is quite an understatement to say he’s had a tough year. He can probably explain it better but the injuries he had and the timing of it has been bad. But now he is fit and we all know what he can bring and he shows it in training and in games as well. It is on him now to keep showing that – hopefully after the World Cup because at the World Cup we play against each other so he can take it a little bit easier then.”

Liverpool’s two most expensive signings ever both scored on Saturday, with Florian Wirtz finding the net in injury time, and Van Dijk feels it is a good sign for the future.

He said: “That was always the plan. These two particular players have been brought to the club to make an impact and it’s not been an easy season for anyone, including those two, but you see the quality they have.”

News.content:

Sir Keir Starmer has insisted that the “vast majority” of Labour MPs support him, despite the scandal over the appointment of Peter Mandelson as US ambassador that has rocked his premiership.

The prime minister faces existential questions about his future in power, but he said he still believes he can win the next election, arguing that most people in the Parliamentary Labour Party is "supportive, loyal and just want to get on with the job”.

Sir Keir has faced calls to resign amid the fallout from the vetting saga, which saw Lord Mandelson take up the role despite security services raising concerns, and Cabinet divisions are said to have emerged over his handling of the process, including his decision to sack Foreign Office chief Sir Olly Robbins.

open image in gallery Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer insisted that the vast majority of MPs support him ( PA Wire )

Meanwhile, Labour MPs are said to be feeling increasingly frustrated by the chaos in government, with many looking to Wes Streeting or Angela Rayner as possible successors to Sir Keir if the local election results are as brutal for the government as expected.

But, speaking to The Times about questions over his future, the prime minister said: "In politics, you get this sort of thing all of the time.

"There is always talk. What you never hear from are all the people who are supportive, loyal and just want to get on with the job. And that is the vast majority of people in the parliamentary Labour Party.

"They’re pleased to be in power. They’ve waited a long time to be in power. And they just want to get on with their job. They don’t make a lot of noise about it. They don’t talk to journalists about it. It’s really important that is reflected in these debates.”

It comes despite polling of Labour members showing that the overwhelming majority think Sir Keir has handled the Mandelson affair badly.

However, around two-thirds (61 per cent) think he should not resign over the scandal, while 29 per cent said he should, the Survation poll for Labour List showed.

They were split on whether Labour should change its leadership, with 46 per cent in favour and 44 per cent saying Sir Keir should remain in post.

In the same interview, the prime minister insisted he thinks he can win the next election, adding: "I think it’s going to be a very important general election. It’s likely to be Labour versus Reform. An election where the defining question is, what is it to be British?

"An election where what I would call patriotic values of tolerance, decency, live and let live, diversity, are under challenge like we’ve never seen before.”

His latest intervention comes after he was accused of breaking the ministerial code by reportedly failing to declare a meeting with a client of Lord Mandelson’s lobbying firm.

According to The Telegraph, the prime minister and Lord Mandelson attended the tech firm Palantir’s headquarters in Washington in February 2025.

They reported that the meeting was not logged, despite ministers being required to publish details of meetings with external organisations as part of the ministerial code.

Downing Street told the newspaper that the event was not a meeting, so it did not need to be recorded. But the Ministry of Defence, which also reportedly attended, described it as a meeting.

Alex Burghart, the shadow chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, accused Sir Keir of breaking the ministerial code, which is widely seen as a resignation offence.

open image in gallery Darren Jones said there is ‘no case to answer’ on a potential Commons sleaze inquiry ( PA )

He added: “The public deserves to know who arranged this meeting, what was discussed, and what Global Counsel’s client stood to gain.”

Next week, the PM is likely to face a Commons vote that could spark an inquiry into his handling of the vetting saga.

The prime minister has repeatedly told MPs that he and his ministers only found out that UKSV had advised that Lord Mandelson should be denied clearance for the role last Tuesday evening, despite The Independent raising concerns that he had failed vetting last September and running a front page story on it.

Speaker Sir Lindsay Hoyle looks set to give MPs a say on whether the prime minister is referred to the powerful Commons Privileges Committee for a probe into whether he misled parliament over the disgraced peer’s appointment.

Sir Lindsay is widely expected to make a statement on the letters on Monday, meaning Sir Keir could face a vote in the Commons on Tuesday – the same day his former chief of staff, Morgan McSweeney, will be grilled by MPs on his role in Lord Mandelson’s appointment.

But Cabinet minister Darren Jones insisted there is “no case to answer” when asked about a potential referral of Sir Keir to a sleaze inquiry, as well as accusing the Conservatives of “using tactics” ahead of local elections.

The minister told the BBC’s Sunday Morning With Laura Kuenssberg programme: “You have to remember, what are these privileges committees about? The last time it was used was when Boris Johnson told the House of Commons there were no parties in Downing Street.

“It was then shown he was at five of them and got a fine from the police. That’s what these processes are in place for, so the Opposition are just using tactics to try to distract from the fact that the government is doing good work in this pre-election period.”

Asked if it would be right to have the investigation and clear up different interpretations of what has happened, Mr Jones added: “As far as I understand the case, there is no case to answer.”

Labour’s huge majority in the Commons means such a vote would almost certainly not pass, but it could still be damaging for the prime minister.

A government spokesperson said: “Firstly, there are robust processes in place to ensure government contracts are awarded fairly and transparently.

“Ministers engage with a range of companies as part of their international travel and Palantir is a longstanding investor in the UK.”
